idiom_name: trait with abstract members (sealed for closed sets); structural type / Selectable for reflection-based contracts
implementation_notes: A Scala trait is the interface construct: abstract defs and vals that every concrete class must implement, mixable into classes that already extend something else, which is what makes a hand-written pure-abstract-class hierarchy unnecessary. Scala is more permissive than Java here - a trait may declare concrete members and parameters - so statelessness is a discipline rather than a compiler rule: keep the contract trait free of fields, or the role silently becomes a base class. Scala 3 adds sealed traits (closed contract sets with exhaustive matching) and structural types (type Closeable = { def close(): Unit }) for contracts over unrelated library types, dispatched through a Selectable instance rather than a declared supertype.
code_sketch:
trait Shape:                      // contract; keep it stateless by convention
  def area: Double

sealed trait Expr                 // closed contract: implementors known
case class Lit(n: Int) extends Expr
case class Add(l: Expr, r: Expr) extends Expr

type Closeable = { def close(): Unit }   // structural contract (reflective dispatch)
pitfalls: Nothing stops a trait from holding state (concrete vals, vars, constructor parameters): once a contract trait acquires a field, trait initialisation order and linearisation leak into every implementation.

Structural types check only what the compiler can prove (in Scala 3 the erased parameter types must agree) and dispatch through reflection or a custom Selectable, so a mismatch fails at run time; Scala 2 additionally needs the reflectiveCalls language import.

Trait linearisation decides which implementation wins when several mixed traits define the same member, and super calls resolve along that order - a frequent source of surprise in wide contract mixes.
